job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Working from the text as provided. Issues are grouped by section, roughly in bill order; a short note on which ones matter most for markup follows the list.

**Sec. 2(1)(A) — Definition threshold**

1. **§2(1)(A), "by a single vessel."** The 10,000 mt/yr threshold is measured per vessel, not per operator, project, or site. An operator can run several vessels each under 10,000 mt, or rotate hulls, and never trigger the prohibition at all.

2. **§2(1)(A), "per year."** "Year" is undefined (calendar, fiscal, rolling 12 months, or license year), and the Act never says who counts the tonnage or how. The threshold is also ambiguous as to wet vs. dry weight (nodules are roughly a third water by mass), landed vs. lifted tonnage, and whether rejected or returned material counts.

3. **§2(1)(A), "recovery … by a single vessel."** In a real nodule operation the collector vehicle, the riser/production vessel, and transshipment bulk carriers are different platforms. The text doesn't say which one "recovers," so an operator can argue the tonnage attributable to any one vessel is below the line.

4. **§2(1)(A), "or other mineral resources."** "Mineral resources" is undefined and read literally captures deepwater oil and gas, sand/gravel, and crusts and sulfides. That overbreadth is a political and litigation vulnerability (it sweeps in Gulf of Mexico OCS production below 200 m) and invites a narrowing construction that could also narrow the nodule coverage.

5. **§2(1)(A), "from the seabed."** No definition of "seabed" or geographic scope: it is unclear whether the Act reaches the U.S. territorial sea, EEZ, and outer continental shelf (where the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act already governs mineral leasing) or only the international Area. Either reading creates a conflict or a gap.

**Sec. 2(1)(B) — Secretary's catch-all**

6. **§2(1)(B), "the Secretary."** "Secretary" is never defined. The only Secretary named in the bill is the Secretary of State (§6), while the registry sits with NOAA (Commerce). As drafted, nobody clearly holds the determination power, so (B) is effectively inoperative.

7. **§2(1)(B), "comparable" risk determination.** The standard is open-ended, has no rulemaking procedure, publication requirement, notice, or judicial-review provision, and feeds directly into criminal liability under §5(b). That is a strong void-for-vagueness / fair-notice challenge and a plausible nondelegation or major-questions argument.

**Sec. 2(2) — U.S. person**

8. **§2(2), entity coverage.** "Corporation organized under the laws of a State" omits LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and other non-corporate forms, and entities organized under federal, D.C., or territorial law. Restructuring the operating entity as a Delaware LLC arguably takes it outside the definition.

9. **§2(2), foreign subsidiaries.** There is no ownership, control, or affiliation attribution. A U.S. corporation can conduct mining through a foreign-incorporated subsidiary and the subsidiary is not a "U.S. person"; the parent is not "engaged" unless a court stretches §3(a).

10. **§2(2), natural persons.** Only citizens are covered; lawful permanent residents and other U.S.-resident individuals abroad are not, which is narrower than comparable extraterritorial statutes (e.g., FCPA, OFAC).

**Sec. 2(3) — Covered vessel**

11. **§2(3), 5,000 GT floor and "equipped."** Vessels at or under 5,000 gross tons are outside the registry entirely, and "equipped for the recovery" is undefined — modular or detachable mining gear lets an operator argue the vessel is not "equipped" when it registers or reports.

12. **§2(3)/§4 vs. §3 mismatch.** The registry keys on vessel size while the prohibition keys on tonnage recovered. A vessel under 5,000 GT could recover more than 10,000 mt and never be required to register or report, so the registry doesn't actually surface the conduct the prohibition targets.

**Sec. 3 — Prohibition and exceptions**

13. **§3(a), "engage in."** The verb is undefined and there is no prohibition on financing, chartering, contracting for, directing, transporting, importing, processing, or selling nodules, and no aiding-and-abetting, conspiracy, or anti-circumvention clause. A U.S. company can finance and offtake from a foreign operator without "engaging" in mining.

14. **§3(a), "person in the United States."** Unclear whether "in the United States" includes the EEZ or vessels on the high seas flying the U.S. flag. "Person" itself is undefined (the Dictionary Act helps, but the bill's own narrower "U.S. person" definition invites an argument that "person" is similarly limited).

15. **§3(a), foreign-flag/foreign-person gap.** Combined with items 9 and 13, a foreign-flagged vessel operated by a foreign entity is outside the Act even if U.S.-owned, U.S.-financed, and U.S.-crewed.

16. **§3(b), grandfather clause.** Any "exploration license issued before the date of enactment" exempts "mining" (undefined, broader than the defined term) with no limit on volume, duration, transfer, renewal, amendment, or expansion of the license. It creates an obvious incentive to obtain licenses before enactment and makes existing licensees permanently exempt.

17. **§3(b), "exploration license" undefined.** It is unclear whether this means only NOAA licenses under the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (DSHMRA) or also ISA exploration contracts and foreign national licenses. Either way, exploration licenses typically don't authorize commercial recovery, so the clause either exempts nothing or exempts everything, and a court will have to pick.

18. **§3(b), cutoff date vs. effective date.** The grandfather cutoff is enactment but the prohibition doesn't take effect until 180 days later (§8), leaving a window where licenses can still be issued, nothing is prohibited, and new licenses are nonetheless not grandfathered — a drafting inconsistency likely to be litigated.

19. **§3(c), environmental assessment exception.** "For the purpose of environmental assessment" has no tonnage cap, duration, approval requirement, data-reporting obligation, or bar on selling recovered material. Commercial-scale test mining is easily characterized as assessment, and the exception doesn't address mixed-purpose activity.

20. **No interaction with DSHMRA.** The bill neither repeals nor amends 30 U.S.C. 1401 et seq., under which NOAA retains authority to issue exploration licenses and commercial recovery permits. That leaves a direct statutory conflict and an argument that permits issued under DSHMRA remain lawful notwithstanding §3.

**Sec. 4 — Registry**

21. **§4, no penalty.** §5 only penalizes violations of §3; failure to register, failure to report, or filing a false report carries no penalty under the Act (only generic 18 U.S.C. 1001 exposure for false statements).

22. **§4, "operator" undefined and no jurisdictional nexus.** The registry nominally applies to every covered vessel in the world regardless of flag or ownership, which is unenforceable against foreign operators and, as drafted, doesn't limit itself to U.S. persons or U.S. waters.

23. **§4, no agency machinery.** NOAA gets no rulemaking authority, deadline, inspection or boarding authority, verification power, data-standard (reports need only "describe" activities, not state tonnage), or funding, and "certified by the operator" has no stated standard or consequence.

**Sec. 5 — Penalties**

24. **§5(a) conflicts with §8.** Civil penalties attach to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but §3 is not effective until 180 days after enactment. Penalizing conduct during the 180-day window is internally contradictory and raises retroactivity/fair-notice objections; at minimum it will be read as unenforceable for that period.

25. **§5(a), "each day on which the violation occurs."** Because the threshold is annual tonnage, it is unclear when a violation "occurs" — the day the 10,000th ton comes up, every day thereafter, or every day of the year. The per-day penalty is hard to calculate and easy to contest.

26. **§5, no enforcement procedure.** The Act names no enforcing agency, no assessment procedure (administrative vs. judicial, notice and hearing), no injunctive relief, no vessel seizure/forfeiture or in rem jurisdiction, no citizen-suit provision, and no statute of limitations (default 28 U.S.C. 2462 would apply).

27. **§5(b), "willfully" plus §2(1)(B).** Criminal liability for conduct defined by an unpublished, standardless Secretary determination is the weakest point in the bill for a constitutional challenge; even without that, "willfully" will be read to require knowledge of unlawfulness, which the undefined terms make hard to prove.

**Sec. 6 — International agreement**

28. **§6, hortatory only.** "Shall seek to negotiate" creates no enforceable duty, no reporting requirement, and no consequence for failure; it also does not address the U.S. non-party status to UNCLOS or the ISA's existing exploration contracts.

**Sec. 7 — Duration**

29. **§7(a), National Academies report.** The lifting mechanism depends on a NAS report that no one is directed or funded to commission, with no deadline, and "serious harm" is undefined. Practically, the prohibition cannot be lifted early.

30. **§7(a) vs. §7(b).** Subsection (a) says the prohibition continues "until Congress … finds" safety; subsection (b) says the whole Act expires in 10 years. The two are inconsistent and (b) controls as the more specific rule, so (a) is largely surplusage.

31. **§7(b), no savings clause.** "This Act shall cease to have effect" sunsets the penalties and registry as well as the prohibition, with no savings provision for pending enforcement actions or violations committed before sunset. Under the common-law abatement rule, unresolved prosecutions and penalty actions may abate.

**Sec. 8 and general**

32. **§8, effective date interactions.** The 180-day delay conflicts with §5(a) (item 24), is not coordinated with §3(b) (item 18), and is unrelated to the §6 18-month diplomatic timeline, so there is no transition logic tying the three together.

33. **No severability clause.** If §2(1)(B) or §5(b) falls on vagueness grounds, there is no textual basis to preserve the rest of the Act.

34. **No rulemaking or appropriations authority anywhere.** No agency is authorized to issue implementing regulations for any section, and nothing is funded, which both hampers enforcement and strengthens a challenge that key terms (items 2, 6, 7) can't be given operative meaning.

---

**Which of these matter most for Thursday:** the structural ones that a manager's second-degree amendment can't easily fix in committee — the per-vessel threshold (1), the U.S.-person/subsidiary gap (8–9, 15), the unlimited grandfather and assessment exceptions (16, 19), the undefined "Secretary" (6), the §5(a)/§8 conflict (24), and the missing DSHMRA conforming amendment (20). The vagueness/criminal issue (7, 27) is the strongest hook if the question is litigation exposure rather than operational workarounds.
